purpose: GPT classifier prompt for evaluating VLM-generated BVL descriptions
usage: Send system + few_shot_examples + one inference_user_turn per generated description
system:
You are an expert annotator for BVL (blind and low-vision) artwork descriptions. Your task is to decompose a given artwork description into atomic clauses and classify each one into exactly one of the following categories:

- Overview: artwork type, main subject, format, setting, medium if known
- Spatial: explicit positional language — left/right, foreground/background, relative size, distance, orientation
- Objects: salient visible subjects, people, items, clothing, actions directly observable in the image
- Visual: color, light, texture, brushwork, material, composition, style — how things look
- VisibleText: verbatim transcription of any legible text, inscription, motto, or label visible in the image
- Interpretation: symbolic, historical, psychological, or moral reading — not directly verifiable from the image alone

For each clause also return:
- visible_fact (boolean): true if the clause describes something directly observable in the image; false if it requires external knowledge, biography, history, or interpretation
- optional_context (boolean): true if the clause should be placed in a separate optional interpretation layer

Split compound sentences at natural clause boundaries. Return a JSON array only — no preamble, no explanation, no markdown.

A man, Georg Gisze, stands shown half-length in a wood-paneled interior, his counting house. A precious Anatolian carpet covers a table in the foreground, on which there are a glass vase with carnations and rosemary, a table clock, a pewter casket for writing implements and various other things. Numerous letters are pinned to the walls; on the shelves hang, to the left, a balance and a seal, and to the right, a splendidly decorated ball of string; books, gold rings, and keys can also be seen. Gisze wears shimmering red silk sleeves, a massive black robe, and a black beret. Without doubt, Gisze himself desired this abundance in order to convey a certain image of himself: the letters point to his activity as a merchant lord, while the precious objects testify to wealth and taste. Gisze’s motto is written on the wall to the left: “Nulla sine merore voluptas” (“No joy without sorrow”). An extravagance such as the red silk of Gisze’s garment may point just as much to the noble rank of the Danzig native as the sword, the pommel of which becomes visible at his left hip. A cartellino at the upper edge of the picture, conceived not as attached to the painted back wall but rather as adhering to the picture surface, contains a Latin distich which in translation reads: “Distich on Georg Gisze. This image, which you see, reproduces Georg’s features; so lively is his eye, so are his cheeks formed / Of his age 34 years / In the year of the Lord 1532.” Gisze opens a letter. It is addressed to his “broder.” The room, like the table, appears not to possess a right angle. Precisely for this reason, however, Gisze appears especially dominant. The persistent fascination exerted by the portrait is due as much to this deviation from what is really possible as to the gaze directed at the viewer with a slight turning of the head—a gaze that seems to scrutinize us in a distant, expectant manner.

Classify this artwork description:

Cranach’s Fountain of Youth lies far from the city, whose towers rise in the background: a rectangular basin, to which steps lead down, situated between mountains and meadows. Women bathe in it. They come along barren stony paths out of an infertile mountain landscape, whose desolation symbolically points to the privations of old age. Helplessly they are brought in on carts or wagons; on stretchers or on people’s backs they are dragged there. At the edge of the basin, young women help them to undress. A doctor casts one last hopeless glance at his patient before she steps into the bath. The characters then prove to be quite varied. Some women boldly step into the bath and resolutely cross it; others sit hesitantly at the edge and need persuasion, or even allow themselves to be pulled in. As frail, ancient hags they step into the basin. There the magical effect of the water unfolds. As the women cross the basin, the wrinkles smooth out, the gray skin tightens and becomes rosy, and at the right-hand edge of the basin they leave the bath as youthful, lovable women. A cavalier receives them and escorts them into a tent, where they are dressed. In new garments and adorned, they join the dance. Cavaliers entertain the women. A table invites them to dine. The company spends a cheerful day with dancing, feasting, and love. On the side of old age one sees rugged, stony mountain land; here, green meadows and fruit-bearing plants in a cheerful pleasure garden. The force that helps the women to new youth comes from the water. What kind of force it is is indicated by the figures on the fountain structure: Cupid, the god of love, and Lady Venus, the goddess of love and beauty, rule over the fountain. Only women bathe in the basin. According to the writer Rabelais, men were rejuvenated through the company of young women and therefore require no transformation. Cranach’s Fountain of Youth is thus a fountain of love.

Classify this artwork description:

The Madonna in the Church is one of the most beautiful and precious works that Jan van Eyck created. A Madonna with the Child in her arm is depicted in a church. The detailed rendering of the architecture and the differentiated gradations of the light lend the church interior an atmosphere of very immediate effect. The impression arises as though one were looking into a timeless world. The light of bright day entering through the clerestory windows and the side portal, casting sun reflections upon the screen walls and the floor of the nave, recalls the passing of time, which nevertheless seems to stand still. In this setting Jan van Eyck has rendered the Mother of God with the Child in supernatural size. She rises above the high arches of the church’s side aisle and is thereby removed from the sphere of human powers of imagination. Since early Christian times Mary had been designated the temple and house of God, since Christ had taken up dwelling in her body as in a temple. Before the high altar in the choir of the church, angels can be discerned singing from an antiphonary. They point to the close relation between sacrament and redemption as well as to the everlasting mass of the end times. If one recalls that all Gothic churches always pointed east with the choir, then it becomes apparent that in our painting the sunlight falls into the church not from the south but, contrary to reality, from the north. It is therefore not natural but eternal light, which follows neither the course of the sun nor that of the stars. This symbolism of light finds its many-layered continuation in the burning candles set up beside the Marian sculpture in the niche of the rood screen. It is striking that the statue corresponds entirely to the Madonna standing before us in lifelike fashion. It appears as though the statue had miraculously been brought to life.
